MX17 at LNL Legnaro · Geant4 feasibility · 8 Oct 2026

MX17 tests the ATOMKI ⁸Be claim at 3σ in ~16 days as built, and in ~1.2 days with big plastics

⁷Li(p,e⁺e⁻)⁸Be at the 18.15 MeV resonance, 1 µA. Geant4 of the full apparatus around a Li₂O target, with a selection that uses no Monte Carlo truth.

16–24 d

n_TOF hardware as built

3σ at R = 5.8×10⁻⁶, 1 µA (counting – template fit); 4–6 d on CN at 4 µA. Needs 3° MM segments or a 0.3 ns time-of-flight veto against cosmics.

1.2–1.6 d

four 75×75×5 cm plastics

The trigger_scint calorimeter option (~€90–140k). 7–10 h on CN at 4 µA.

3.3 % → 23 %

X17 pairs triggered

Both leptons reach the Micromegas in 39 % of decays; the two 20×30 cm plastics per arm are the bottleneck.

1

Details

Geant4 on the MX17_Full_Geant lnl branch (runs L1–L6, overnight 2026-10-08): X17 at four masses, Born IPC M1/E1 at 18.15, 17.64, 15.1 and 14.6 MeV, γ lines, one live day of cosmics, a chamber/backing scan, for the n_TOF stack as built and with four 75×75×5 cm plastics. Analysis: lnl/sim/lnl_geant.py; write-up lnl/FEASIBILITY_SIM.md; this deck reads lnl/out/geant/*.csv.

The days use counting in the best window (typically 130–165°) and an Asimov template fit over 90–180° with the IPC and γ₁ normalisations free (the M1/E1 mix fixed); with the mix also free the fit is ×2.3–3 slower. Rates and yields are lnl_rates.py.

2

Details

Arms going outward: air; Micromegas TPC (30 mm drift, 60 µm aluminised mylar window, active area 399.4 × 359.9 mm, faces at ±204 mm); SiPM scintillator wall; two 20 × 30 × 2 cm plastic bars; liquid scintillators. The real layout is a pinwheel, which the drawing leaves out; the toy acceptance uses plain planes at 204 mm.

Kinematics: the ⁸Be* recoils at β ≈ 0.006, which is negligible. The X17 edge (θ_min = 2·asin(m_X/E_X)) is 133.8–138.9° for m = 16.7–17.0 MeV at E_p = 1.03 MeV (out/kinematics.csv).

The beam is easy: both LNL Van de Graaffs cover the window

Energy range of the two machines against the ⁸Be resonances. Hover the bars and the lines.

Both machines cover it. 0.44–1.23 MeV is the whole programme: the two resonances and the off-resonance points ATOMKI and Hanoi used.

No neutrons below 1.88 MeV, so the current is limited by the target, not by radiation protection.

LNL already did this: the Marchi / Góngora-Servín spectrometer ran on AN2000 in 2023–24. Unpublished; they are the first people to talk to.

Access: the yearly LNL PAC (autumn). Contacts: A. Selva, pacbeams@lnl.infn.it.

Source: LNL beam sheet (2025 PAC call), CN paper arXiv:2605.12005. lnl/FACILITY.md

Details

From LNL's own beam sheet (lnl/refs/LNL_Beams_AN2000_CN.txt) and the 2026 CN paper (arXiv:2605.12005). Details, open questions and contacts are in lnl/FACILITY.md.

At 1.1 MeV, half the γ₀ is direct capture, not the resonance

⁷Li(p,γ₀)⁸Be cross section split into the two M1 resonances and a flat E1 direct capture. Hover the points.

total σ(γ₀), Zahnow 1995

M1 resonances

direct E1 capture

52 % of the γ₀ is direct E1 capture in ATOMKI's 2016 anomaly run (Li₂O 300 µg/cm² at 1.10 MeV); the 18.15 resonance makes the rest.

That matters: E1 IPC has ~2.5× the M1 rate at 140°, and ATOMKI 2022 sees its excess in direct capture too.

The 441 keV resonance is 50× stronger and makes 17.64 MeV pairs, where MEG II already limits X17. A thick target walks into it.

lnl/out/figures/excitation.csv (lnl_rates.py). Curves below 1 µb are drawn at 1 µb.

4

Details

Zahnow et al. 1995 (EXFOR A0639) S-factors for γ₀ and γ₀+γ₁, 98–1500 keV, converted to σ. The resonances are Breit–Wigner with constant widths (Tilley 2004); direct capture is the remainder. The split is not meaningful below ~500 keV, where the BW tail and the data disagree, but it is harmless at 1 MeV.

Checks against Tilley: σ(γ₀+γ₁) at 441 keV = 5.93 mb (5.9 ± 0.5); γ₀/(γ₀+γ₁) = 0.69 (0.69–0.72). MEG II's own 2026 normalisation is reproduced when their n and σ are used (factor 2 in the inputs, not the method).

X17 pairs open to ≥ 134°; the edge moves with E_p

θ_min = 2·asin(m_X/E_X) against E_p, for three masses. Hover the points.

16.85

17.0

The X17 piles up above an edge at 134–139° at the 18.15 resonance; IPC falls steeply there.

The edge moves by ~10° over the scanned energies, so a real signal must follow it. That is the test the off-resonance points make.

The Geant4 reach uses the window that maximises S/√B (~130–165°) and a template fit over 90–180°; the edge sits inside both for all three masses.

Keep the film thin (≲ 300 µg/cm² ≈ 60 keV of energy loss): then < 1 % of the γ₀ is 17.64 MeV, and the signal sits at 18.15.

A beam that stops in Li metal at 1.10 MeV gets 77 % of its γ₀ from 441 keV. That is what happened to ATOMKI's 2016 targets (Sas 2022).

Use boron-free Li: ¹¹B(p,γ) puts 16–17 MeV γ in the window. LiF gives a free ¹⁹F E0 line (6.05 MeV) for calibration.

Details

Thin-target yields from the Zahnow σ and PSTAR stopping (Li by Bragg subtraction), integrated through the film (lnl_rates.thin_yield). Recommendation (lnl/TARGETS.md): a few-hundred-nm film of LiF or Li₂O (or Li metal, or sputtered LiPON) on a 10–25 µm Al/C/Cu foil, in a thin carbon-fibre chamber. Heat at 1 µA is ~0.06 W in a 300 µg/cm² film.

Geometry is fine: both leptons reach the active Micromegas in 39 % of X17 decays (the toy said 45 %).

The trigger keeps 3.3 %. The two 20×30×2 cm plastics per arm cover a fraction of the Micromegas cone. Four 75×75×5 cm slabs keep 23 %.

7

Details

An arm is "ok" with a trigger leg (a SiPM bar AND a plastic, each ≥ 0.5 MIP) and a Micromegas segment whose charge centroid is in the active area. Pairs = the two ok arms with most scintillator energy. The arm choice matches the true lepton arms in 99.8 % of X17 events. The pre-Geant4 toy multiplied geometry by EPS_REST = 0.14 from the ILL; the real factor here is 0.084 as built.

The accepted X17 spreads from the 134° edge to 170°: the four-arm geometry favours back-to-back pairs, so only ~64 % of the tagged pairs fall in 125–155°. The template fit uses the rest.

8

Details

The pre-Geant4 estimate assumed the n_TOF stack (~40 % containment) could not separate the γ₁ transitions (to the 3.0 MeV state, W ≈ 15 MeV, twice as frequent as γ₀) and counted their IPC in full. Geant4 says the LS make the difference: with them, nothing from 15.1 MeV reaches 13 MeV. The LS suffered pile-up at n_TOF; at LNL the rates are ~10³× lower, but whether they can be read is to be checked (ask). "As built, LS off": the window cannot exclude γ₁, and the reach goes from 15 to 19 days.

lnl/out/geant/cosmics_*.csv

9

Details

Cosmic μ± from a 3×3 m plane, 1 /cm²/min, zenith perpendicular to the beam (sea level, no overburden). MEG II members showed in 2026 that cosmic two-arm coincidences make a ~140° bump in ATOMKI-type spectrometers; this is that effect quantified for MX17. Entries ≤ 2 are single events in one live day. The pointing cut keeps 90 % of X17 segments per arm (D = 135 mm at 15°, 57 mm at 3°; scattering in the window and gas sets the 3° value). σ_t = 0.3 ns per arm is an assumption (ask): at 1 ns the veto no longer separates the 2.3 ns muon delay. Two-arm cosmic triggers: 3.5/s as built, 22/s with big plastics; DREAM stays > 99 % live.

Details

Counting: d = 9·B/S² in the window that maximises S/√B (130–165° typically). A month reaches below the ATOMKI claim; with big plastics, ×5 below

The X17 ratio R on one log axis: ATOMKI's claim, MEG II's null, and MX17's 3σ reach after 30 days at 1 µA (Geant4). Hover the points.

The record is contradictory. ATOMKI (2016, 2022) and Hanoi (2024) see ~140° excesses; MEG II (2025) sees nothing; MEG II members (Sept 2026) show cosmics make a 140° bump in ATOMKI-type spectrometers.

What MX17 adds: tracks + timing that remove cosmics, and with big plastics ~9× ATOMKI's pair acceptance (as built, about equal: 3.3 % vs ~2.5 %). LNL's own 2023–24 data (unpublished) are the other result to wait for.

MX17 points: lnl/out/geant/reach_geant.csv (MM 15° + TOF).

Appendix · the basics, for someone new to proton beams

How a proton-beam X17 measurement works, from the accelerator to the opening angle

every acronym in the deck

The short answers

Beam: one energy you dial in (0.2–2 MeV on AN2000), ~1 keV wide, continuous, 6×10¹² protons/s per µA. No neutrons below 1.88 MeV.

Target: thin, so the beam spends only 1.10 → 1.04 MeV in lithium. A target that stops the beam makes 77 % of its pairs at 17.64 MeV, where there is no X17.

Chamber: needed for the vacuum; its wall sets the angular resolution (5.1° for 0.4 mm CFRP). ~4° is reachable with a thinner or wider wall.

Physics: like ³He, capture then de-excitation. No useful boost (β = 0.006); the X17's own speed sets the ~134° edge, which drops as E_p rises. Off resonance is a test, not more X17.

15

Details

Written 2026-10-08 for readers new to the ⁸Be channel and to proton beams. Everything quantitative comes from lnl_rates.py (cross sections, stopping, yields), lnl/appendix_calc.py (depth profiles, scattering model, decay kinematics, off-resonance yields) or the Geant4 tables of the main deck. Analytic stand-ins are labelled as such.

A Van de Graaff gives one proton energy, set by a voltage

Schematic of a single-ended electrostatic accelerator like AN2000 or CN (not to scale). Hover the parts.

Choose any E_p in 0.2–2.0 MeV on AN2000 (0.8–5.5 on CN). Self-service AN2000: one change per day, which suits a plan of a few energies held for days.

Continuous (DC): protons arrive at random, 6.2×10¹² /s at 1 µA. CN can also pulse: 2 ns every 333 ns (≤ 700 nA).

Energy calibration on known narrow lines: the 441 keV resonance itself, ²⁷Al(p,γ) at 992 keV, the ⁷Li(p,n) threshold at 1.881 MeV.

Main slide 3 (Beam) gives the machine ranges. lnl/FACILITY.md

16

Details

An electrostatic accelerator keeps one electrode (the terminal) at a steady high voltage V. Ions are made inside the terminal and fall to ground through the accelerating tube, gaining q·V. For protons (q = e), E_p in MeV equals V in MV. There is no RF and no bunching, so the beam is continuous.

The analysing magnet is what fixes the energy precisely. It passes only one momentum per charge onto the slits, and the slit currents correct V. The LNL sheet quotes σ_E/E ~ 10⁻³ for CN (~1 keV at 1 MeV); AN2000 is not quoted (ask), but it is the same kind of machine. 1 keV is small compared to the target thickness (~60 keV in 300 µg/cm² Li₂O) and to the 168 keV width of the 18.15 MeV resonance, though not to the 12 keV of the 441 keV one.

Contamination: the source also makes H₂⁺ (two protons at E/2 each) and H₃⁺. A properly tuned analysing magnet removes them. MEG II's Cockcroft–Walton beam had 25 % H₂⁺ and put most of its data on 441 keV (TARGETS.md §6). Specify H⁺ only.

Sources: LNL beam sheet (refs/LNL_Beams_AN2000_CN.txt), CN paper arXiv:2605.12005, lnl/FACILITY.md.

One energy at a time, all the time: the opposite of n_TOF

Left: energies each beam delivers (log scale). Right: when the particles arrive. Hover the bars.

No time of flight needed: E_p is known from the machine. The only energy spread that matters is the ~60 keV lost in the film.

Beam off = pure cosmics: with a DC beam you measure the cosmic background directly by switching the beam off.

CN pulsed: a pair must arrive in a 2 ns window every 333 ns, a ×~50 cut on cosmics.

LNL beam sheet; CN paper arXiv:2605.12005. Energy bands are ranges, not flux shapes.

17

Details

Energy. n_TOF gives every energy at once and sorts them afterwards by time of flight; most of the beam is at energies the X17 does not want. The ILL gives one energy (thermal). LNL gives one energy that we choose. There is no "yield spectrum" of the beam itself: it is a line. What has a spectrum is the reaction as the beam slows inside the target (A6, and main slide 4 for σ(E_p)).

Time. A continuous beam means no beam-off window to measure cosmics in, but also no instantaneous rate spikes: at 1 µA the two-arm trigger rate is a few per second, dominated by cosmics (main slide 12). CN's pulsed mode is a cosmic and accidental veto nobody has used for ⁸Be yet (a pair must arrive in the 2 ns window): ×~50 against cosmics in PHYSICS.md §4.

n_TOF numbers are the facility's standard ones (20 GeV/c PS bunches of ~7 ns, ≥ 1.2 s apart); they are here only for contrast.

Protons stop in microns: thin targets, vacuum, no neutrons

What changes when the beam is protons instead of neutrons. Hover the dotted terms.

neutrons (n_TOF, ILL)protons (LNL)
what the beam does in the targetno charge: flies straight until it is captured or scattersionises continuously: loses ~20 keV per 100 µg/cm², stops in ~17 µm of Al
so the target isthick: the ILL ³He cell absorbs 99.5 % of the beamthin: a ~1.5 µm film that only ~60 keV of the beam energy is spent in; the beam goes on to a dump
fraction of beam that makes a 20 MeV γ1.03×10⁻⁸ per absorbed n3.0×10⁻¹⁰ per proton (γ₀)
20 MeV-class γ per second~196/s at the ILL (1.9×10¹⁰ n/s absorbed)~1,848/s at 1 µA (γ₀ only; γ₁ adds 2×)
why the cross section is smallradiative capture competes with (n,p), which is 10⁸× biggerCoulomb barrier: σ(p,γ₀) ~ 20–30 µb near 1 MeV
beam-made background in the detectoryes, the dominant one: stray neutrons captured everywhere (MM occupancy, accidentals)almost none: no neutrons below 1.881 MeV; γ from other nuclei (¹⁹F, ²⁷Al, ¹¹B) and the dump. Cosmics dominate.
beam pathair or He is fine; windowsvacuum all the way to the target, so a chamber wall the leptons must cross (B3)
normalisationflux monitors, simulated beam profilethe charge on the Faraday cup: protons counted directly
what wears outthe gas cell leaks ³He1.1 W/µA of heat, implanted hydrogen, Li diffusion: replace targets ~weekly

18

Details

The headline difference is that a proton beam interacts with every electron it passes, so it slows down and stops, while a neutron beam passes through matter almost freely until it is captured. Three consequences run through the whole deck:

  1. The target has to be thin, and its thickness sets which ⁸Be energies are made (B1).
  2. The beam has to be in vacuum, so there is a chamber whose wall scatters the leptons (B3–B4).
  3. The beam does not fill the hall with neutrons. At the ILL the stray neutrons set the walls on rate (MM occupancy, accidentals). Here the beam-related background is tiny and the cosmics are what is left (main slides 9 and 12).

The ILL rate is R_MAX 1.9×10¹⁰ n/s (the Ø2 cm spot) × 1.03×10⁻⁸; the ILL also has the M1/E0 pair channels at a similar α. The LNL rate is the ATOMKI-2016 target at 1 µA from out/yields.csv. Ranges: PSTAR (lnl/data/pstar_stopping.csv). ILL numbers: ill/FEASIBILITY_SIM.md.

Every step after the γ₀ is a fixed fraction of it. That is why the main deck counts photons: γ₀ per second is the unit everything scales with (B2).

19

Details

Each bar is the previous physics bar times one factor. Protons → γ₀ is the thin-target yield (cross section × ⁷Li atoms per cm², integrated as the beam slows through the film). γ₀ → IPC is the Born internal-conversion coefficient α at 18.15 MeV (out/ipc_alpha.csv), weighted by the resonance (M1) and direct-capture (E1) shares. γ₀ → X17 is the ATOMKI ratio R. The detector bars are the Geant4 chain of main slide 7 and the per-day budget of main slide 10.

A stopping target walks the beam through 441 keV

Main slide 6 explained. Top: the two targets. Left: proton energy against depth. Right: where that puts the beam on σ(E_p).

lnl/out/appendix/depth.csv, lnl/out/figures/excitation.csv, lnl/out/yields.csv

20

Details

"Stopping" refers to the proton beam, not to photons. A stopping (or "thick") target is one in which the protons lose all their energy. A thin target lets them through having lost only a little. Slide 6 asks: of the 18 MeV-class photons the target makes, how many come from the 441 keV resonance (and so are 17.64 MeV transitions, not 18.15)?

The answer depends only on which proton energies are spent inside lithium. In the thin film the protons go from 1100 to 1039 keV, nowhere near 441, so 0.6 % of γ₀ are 17.64 (the BW tail). In a target that stops the beam, every energy down to zero is spent in lithium. The 441 keV resonance is only 12 keV wide, but its peak is ~50× the 18.15 one, so it ends up making 77 % of all γ₀. Thin: 1,848 γ₀/s, 0.6 % at 17.64 MeV. Stopping: 143,074 γ₀/s, 77 % at 17.64 MeV.

This happened to ATOMKI in 2016: their "300 µg/cm² Li₂O" was really metallic Li diffused ~10 µm into the Al backing (Sas 2022). The fix is a stable compound (LiF, Li₂O) on a cool backing, checked during the run (478 keV PIGE line, γ₀ line width).

Curves: out/appendix/depth.csv (PSTAR stopping, the integration of lnl_rates.thin_yield). Li metal at 0.534 g/cm³; the Li₂O film at bulk density, 300 µg/cm² = 1.49 µm.

Every pair channel is a fixed fraction of the photons

What an excited ⁸Be nucleus does next, per 18 MeV photon. Hover the branches.

We never count the photons themselves. We count γ₀ because both the background (IPC = α·γ₀) and the signal (X17 = R·γ₀) are fixed fractions of it. Double the γ₀, double both.

So "77 % of γ₀ at 17.64 MeV" means 77 % of the pairs come from the wrong state. 17.64 MeV makes IPC (α = 3.4e-03) but no X17 (MEG II: R(17.6) < 1.8×10⁻⁶).

The energy sum cannot tell them apart: 17.64 and 18.15 are 0.5 MeV apart, well inside the E_sum resolution. For the same X17 a stopping target gives ×4.4 the IPC.

Tilley 2004 (A = 8); lnl/out/ipc_alpha.csv; lnl/PHYSICS.md §1

21

Details

Slides 6 and 10 of the main deck express target yields as "γ₀ per second". γ₀ is the transition to the ⁸Be ground state. It is what earlier experiments measured (Zahnow's σ(p,γ₀)), and it is the denominator of R = Γ_X/Γ_γ. The pairs follow from it: IPC is α·γ₀ with α ≈ 3.5–4.4×10⁻³ (Born, out/ipc_alpha.csv), X17 is R·γ₀.

The fraction of γ₀ from the 441 keV resonance is the fraction of the pair background that comes with no X17. That holds for ATOMKI's 2016 non-observation at 17.64 and MEG II's limit there. With 77 % of the IPC coming from 17.64, the signal-to-background in the window drops by ×4.4, and the IPC shape changes (pure M1, no E1).

γ₁ (to the broad 3.0 MeV state) is twice as frequent but 3 MeV lower. The E_sum window removes it (main slide 8).

The beam needs vacuum, and the leptons pay for the wall

Side view of the Geant4 target region with one X17 lepton crossing the chamber wall. Hover the parts.

Why a chamber at all: the beam must be in vacuum. A 1.1 MeV proton stops in ~2.7 cm of air; the film would oxidise; the beam line is pumped anyway.

What it costs: each lepton crosses the wall and scatters, by 2.6° rms in 0.4 mm CFRP and 5.5° in 0.5 mm Al (Highland, 8.6 MeV). The opening angle is the chord from the beam spot to the hit, so the kink becomes an angle error.

Geant4 (L5): X17 σ68 = 5.1° (CFRP 0.4), 8.8° (Al 0.5), 12.2° (Al 1.0). The wall is the largest single term; acceptance does not change.

The backing and holder matter less: a Cu 25 µm backing gives 7.5°, C 20 µm the same as Al 10 µm.

Geant4 L5 chamber scan: lnl/out/geant/material_scan.csv. Highland: PDG formula, plane-projected, β = 1.

22

Details

Geometry (MX17_Full_Geant lnl, --target li): Li₂O 300 µg/cm² film on Al 10 µm, Al 1 mm holder annulus at r 10–20 mm, CFRP 0.4 mm chamber tube of inner radius 25 mm and half-length 300 mm, Al 5 mm flanges, Ta 2 mm dump at +250 mm. The leptons of an X17 pair leave at ~25–155° to the beam, so each crosses the tube wall once, at ~68° on average, over a path of t/sin θ.

Why it matters: the X17 makes a sharp edge in the opening angle at ~134°. A resolution σ smears the edge over ~σ, so the analysis window has to be wider and lets more IPC in. Main slide 12 has the scan; B4 extrapolates it to other walls.

The Micromegas measure positions well (0.6–0.8 mm) and directions poorly (11–26°), so the opening angle is reconstructed as the chord from the beam spot (a point, here) to the hit. A kink at radius r moves the hit by θ·(L − r), an angle error of θ·(L − r)/L at the Micromegas (L ≈ 215 mm).

The wall can come down from 5.1° to ~4°, never below 3.5°

The floor is 3.5° with no wall at all: the beam spot, air, the Micromegas window and gas, the backing. Past ~4° the wall is no longer the main term.

Thinner or lighter wall: CFRP 0.2 mm or Be 0.25 mm → ~4.3°. A thin Kapton window band in the lepton path → ~3.7°, but it must hold vacuum over the band (engineering to check).

Wider tube: the kink happens closer to the Micromegas, so it matters less. r = 100 mm → ~4.2°. It does not cost acceptance.

Avoid Al anywhere between the film and the arms (×2 on σ).

lnl/out/appendix/highland.csv (model) and lnl/out/geant/material_scan.csv (Geant4 L5).

23

Details

Model (lnl/appendix_calc.py, an analytic stand-in until Geant4 runs these walls): σ68² = s₀² + (k·θ₀·(L − r)/L)², with θ₀ the Highland angle of an 8.6 MeV lepton in the wall (normal incidence), L = 215 mm and r the wall radius. s₀ = 3.48° and k = 1.67 are fitted to the three Geant4 walls (CFRP 0.4, Al 0.5, Al 1.0) and reproduce them to 0.1°. X₀: CFRP 27.5 cm (carbon at 1.55 g/cm³), Al 8.9, Be 35.3, Kapton 28.6 cm.

Not modelled: the oblique path (×1/sin θ, the same for every option, so it is in k), a window band's frame, and how much reach a better σ buys. The last needs the Geant4 reach machinery (sim/lnl_geant.py) on new L5-type runs. Worth doing before designing the chamber. The ATOMKI and MEG II chambers are carbon-fibre tubes (Ø48 mm, 400 µm); the LNL group's chamber drawings are (ask).

Like ³He: a capture, then a de-excitation

Level schemes (simplified) of ⁸Be and ⁴He, with the capture entry point and the transitions we look at. Hover the levels.

Yes, the same premise. Capture makes an excited nucleus (⁸Be* here, ⁴He* at n_TOF). It de-excites to the ground state by a photon, by IPC, or (the claim) by an X17.

Difference 1: the Coulomb barrier. The neutron is captured at any energy, even at rest. The proton needs ~MeV and is captured mostly where a ⁸Be state sits: the resonances.

Difference 2: which state you make is chosen by E_p. On a resonance you make one 1⁺ state; between them, direct capture. At n_TOF E_n sets E* too, but the beam is white.

Difference 3: the ⁸Be ground state breaks into 2α, harmless, at 92 keV total.

Tilley et al., NPA 745 (2004); lnl/PHYSICS.md §1

24

Details

Energies from Tilley 2004 (A = 8) and the ⁴He compilation; only the levels that matter here are drawn. The excitation is the binding of the projectile (Q = 17.2551 MeV for p + ⁷Li, S_n = 20.577 MeV for n + ³He) plus the centre-of-mass kinetic energy, which is the lab energy × M_target/(M_target + m_projectile): 7/8 here, 3/4 at n_TOF.

The two ⁸Be 1⁺ levels differ in isospin. 17.64 is mostly T = 1 and 18.15 mostly T = 0 (mixed ~95/5 %). ATOMKI's anomaly is in the isoscalar one and absent in the isovector one, which is part of why theorists care (a protophobic vector boson couples differently to the two).

E* = 17.255 MeV from the masses + ⅞ of the beam energy

The energy bookkeeping of one capture, to scale above 17 MeV. Hover each step.

① The masses. ⁷Li plus a proton weigh 17.255 MeV more than ⁸Be. Merging them releases that, even with the proton at rest: the "Q value".

② The beam adds on top. Energy is conserved, so the proton's kinetic energy joins the pot. More E_p, more energy in the ⁸Be*: that is all "more beam energy gives a higher E*" means.

③ Only ⅞ of it counts. The proton brings momentum; the merged ⁸Be* must carry it, so it moves, and that motion costs E_p·m_p/(m_p+m_Li) ≈ E_p/8. A ball thrown into a parked cart: they roll on together; only the rest becomes heat.

E_p [keV]to motionto E*E* [MeV]

80010070017.955
103012990118.156
1225154107118.326

Tilley et al., NPA 745 (2004); lnl/out/appendix/energy.csv

25

Details

The rule. Energy and momentum are both conserved when the proton and the ⁷Li merge. Before: a proton with kinetic energy E_p and momentum p, a ⁷Li at rest, and the extra mass Q = m(p) + m(⁷Li) − m(⁸Be) = 17.255 MeV. After: a single ⁸Be*, which must carry the momentum p, so it moves with kinetic energy p²/(2M₈) = E_p·m_p/M₈ ≈ E_p/8. What is left is the internal (excitation) energy:

E* = Q + E_p · M(⁷Li)/(M(⁷Li) + m_p) = 17.255 + 0.875 · E_p

The 0.875·E_p is the centre-of-mass energy: the kinetic energy seen by someone riding along with the centre of mass, the only frame in which the merged nucleus ends at rest. Physicists quote resonances in either frame; the deck uses lab E_p because that is what the accelerator sets (441 keV lab = 386 keV cm).

Same at n_TOF: E* = S_n + 0.75·E_n, because ³He is 3 mass units and the neutron 1 (¾ instead of ⅞). S_n = 20.577 MeV is the same "masses" term. A thermal neutron brings ~0 kinetic energy, so the ILL makes ⁴He* right at 20.58 MeV.

The proton has a minimum it needs, the neutron does not. The Coulomb barrier (≈1.3 MeV between p and ⁷Li) makes capture rare below a few hundred keV; it falls off exponentially but is never zero (tunnelling). That is a probability statement (C1b), not an energy one: the bookkeeping above holds at any E_p.

Numbers: out/appendix/energy.csv from appendix_calc.energy_table (relativistic; the ⅛ is exact to 0.1 %). Masses: AME2020 via lnl_rates.py; Q from Tilley 2004 (17.2551 MeV).

Any E_p makes ⁸Be*; the resonances are where it is likely

Capture cross section to the ground state against E_p (bottom) and the E* it makes (top). Hover the points and bands.

total γ₀ (measured)

17.64 resonance

18.15 resonance

direct capture

Levels this high are not sharp. They fall apart in ~10⁻²¹ s, nearly always by throwing the proton back out. A short life means a spread in energy, the width Γ. An E* within ~Γ of a level still forms it.

Between levels, capture still happens: the proton is caught directly and radiates on the way in (E1). ~19 µb, against 33 µb on the 18.15 peak and 4.0 mb on 17.64.

Either way, energy is exact. The ⁸Be* forms at E* = 17.255 + ⅞E_p, whatever E_p is, and the photon (or pair, or X17) leaves with it: 17.93 MeV at 0.80, 18.30 at 1.225.

Like a radio dial: you can tune to any frequency (E_p); the stations (levels) are where the signal is loud. 17.64 is a sharp, loud station; 18.15 a broad one, heard over ±80 keV of E_p.

Zahnow et al., Z. Phys. A 351 (1995) via EXFOR A0639; Tilley et al., NPA 745 (2004)

26

Details

A common confusion. If ⁸Be has levels at 17.64 and 18.15 MeV, how can E* take any value in between? Because the states above the p + ⁷Li threshold (17.255 MeV) are unbound: the proton can leave again, and almost always does (Γ_p = 132 of the 138 keV width of the 18.15 level; the photon width is only 1.9 eV). Anything that lives ~10⁻²¹ s has an energy spread ħ/τ ≈ Γ. So a "level" is a bump in probability, not a single allowed energy.

The cross section σ is that probability (per proton, per ⁷Li per cm²). The curve is ATOMKI-independent data (Zahnow 1995), split into two Breit–Wigner resonances and a smooth remainder, the direct E1 capture (main slide 4). Resonant capture: the proton enters, a ⁸Be* lingers briefly at the level, then decays. Direct capture: the proton emits the photon as it passes, with no intermediate state; it has no peak, just a slow rise as the Coulomb barrier gets easier.

What the beam energy does, then: it sets E* exactly (C1a) and, through σ, how often a capture happens at all. On the 18.15 peak about half of the γ₀ is resonant (M1) and half direct (E1); at 0.80 MeV almost all is direct. This is why off-resonance runs (C6) test whether the X17 comes from the 1⁺ state or from any transition at that E*.

In a real target the beam slows as it crosses the film, so a thin film at 1.10 MeV spans E_p 1.10 → 1.04 MeV, i.e. E* 18.22 → 18.17 MeV: a 52 keV spread of photon energies, well inside the 18.15 level. A target that stops the beam spans everything down to 0 and so also crosses 441 keV (B1).

Curves: out/figures/excitation.csv (lnl_rates.CrossSection). Widths from Tilley 2004; Γ_lab = Γ_cm × 8/7. The direct-capture curve is drawn from 500 keV: under the 441 keV peak it cannot be separated from the resonance.

Only E* − m ≈ 1.5 MeV moves the X17, so E_p has leverage

Left: the X17 energy split into mass and motion (m = 16.7 MeV). Right: the decay at the edge, slow vs fast X17.

E_p 441 → 1225 keV raises E* by only 685 keV (3.9 %), but almost all of the X17's energy is its mass. The part left over to move it grows by 73 %.

Faster X17, more forward push on both leptons, smaller angle between them. The sideways part is fixed by the mass (m/2 each), so the edge is a mass measurement once E* is known.

Why IPC does not move: a virtual photon has no fixed mass; its pairs take every opening angle, peaked at small ones. Only a real particle has an edge to move.

lnl/out/appendix/energy.csv

27

Details

The chain. The X17 (if it exists) is emitted by the ⁸Be*, which sits nearly at rest (β ≈ 0.006, C4). The ⁸Be ground state is 7455 MeV heavy and takes almost no recoil, so the X17 gets essentially all of E*: E_X = E* − ~0.003 MeV. Of that, m = 16.7 MeV is rest mass; only the leftover E_X − m is kinetic energy, and it sets the speed: β = √(1 − (m/E_X)²).

The leverage. Because E_X − m is small, a small change in E* is a big fractional change in kinetic energy: 0.94 MeV at 441 keV, 1.45 at 1030, 1.62 at 1225. The speed goes 0.32 → 0.39 → 0.41. A heavier X17 (m = 17.0) has even less left over (1.15 MeV at 1030 keV) and opens wider, 139° instead of 134°.

The angle. In the X17 frame the e⁺ and e⁻ leave back to back with p* = √((m/2)² − m_e²) = 8.35 MeV/c each. The edge (smallest lab angle) is the decay perpendicular to the X17 motion: each lepton keeps its 8.35 MeV/c sideways and gains γβ·m/2 forward, so tan(θ_min/2) = p*/(γβ·m/2), i.e. θ_min = 2·asin(m/E_X). A photon is the limit m → 0: no rest mass, all motion, θ → 0, which is why IPC pairs crowd at small angles.

Numbers: out/appendix/energy.csv (lnl_rates.x17_energy, theta_min); main slide 5 plots θ_min against E_p for three masses; C5 shows the full distributions.

M1, E1, E0: what the transition carries off

Left: the three kinds of transition. Right: IPC opening-angle shapes at 18.15 MeV, Born, 4π. Hover the cards and points.

Here: direct capture (s-wave proton, l = 0), ~half the γ₀ at 1.1 MeV. α = 4.4e-03. Pairs spread to larger angles.

Here: only the ¹⁹F(p,α)¹⁶O 6.05 MeV calibration line (LiF). At n_TOF/ILL: the ⁴He E0 branch.

M1 IPC

E1 IPC

28

Details

The "multipolarity" of a transition is the angular momentum L and parity the emitted photon carries away. An electric transition (EL) changes parity by (−1)^L; a magnetic one (ML) by (−1)^(L+1). The initial and final spins and parities fix which ones are allowed, and the lowest allowed one wins. Here the final state is always the 0⁺ ground state (or the 2⁺ for γ₁).

The same rules apply when the photon is virtual and makes a pair (IPC). Each multipolarity then has its own opening-angle distribution. All of them peak at small angles (the pair "remembers" it was almost a real photon), but E1 falls more slowly. At 140° an E1 transition makes 2.9× more pairs per photon than an M1. This is why the direct-capture (E1) share matters for the background: main slide 4, and C6.

Curves: Born IPC from nTof_x17 ipc_born through lnl_rates.py, generated (before the detector), the "(generated)" columns of out/acceptance_hist.csv. A real transition can be an M1–E1 mixture with interference, which changes the shape. That is open item 3 in HANDOFF.md.

What we look for: a 7 % step at the edge of the IPC

Opening angle at the ATOMKI-2016 point, 4π (no detector), per 10⁶ γ₀. Left: log scale. Right: the ratio. Hover the points.

lnl/out/acceptance_hist.csv, ipc_alpha.csv, yields.csv

29

Details

This is the measurement in one picture. The IPC falls by ~100× from small angles to 140°. The X17 is emitted with a fixed energy, so its pairs pile up just above a kinematic edge (C4) and show up as a step of ~7 % over the IPC at R = 5.8×10⁻⁶. ATOMKI's 2016 plot is this, after their detector acceptance.

The detector reshapes both curves (main slide 7: the four arms favour back-to-back pairs, and the trigger keeps a few %), and γ₁ IPC and cosmics add to the background (main slides 8–9). What the analysis needs: the IPC shape known well enough (M1/E1 mix) that a few-% step is not a shape error. That is why the main slides fit a template over 90–180° and why ATOMKI calibrate on the pure-M1 441 keV line.

Weights: IPC = γ₀ × [(f_res) α_M1 shape_M1 + (f_direct) α_E1 shape_E1], with f_direct = 0.52 (Li₂O 300, 1.10 MeV); X17 = γ₀ × R × shape_X17 (m = 16.7, W = 18.15). Shapes from out/acceptance_hist.csv (generated).

The X17's own speed (β = 0.39) sets the angle, not the recoil

Left: an X17 decay at rest and in the lab. Right: lab opening angle against the decay angle, for three E*. Hover the points.

E* 17.64

18.15

18.33 (E_p 1.225)

No useful boost along the beam: the ⁸Be* recoils at β = 0.0059 at 1.03 MeV. It changes the X17 opening angle by 0.32° on average (99 % < 0.6°), against a 5° resolution. At n_TOF the ⁴He* moves at β = 0.016 (2 MeV) to 0.043 (14 MeV).

The edge is where the decay is ⊥ to the X17 motion, and half of all decays (|cos θ*| < 0.5) land within 5.6° of it. That pile-up is the bump of C3.

30

Details

The X17 is heavy compared to the energy available: m = 16.7 MeV out of E* = 18.15 MeV, so it moves at only β = 0.39 (γ = 1.087). In its own frame the e⁺ and e⁻ fly apart back to back, 8.35 MeV/c each. In the lab its motion pushes both forward, closing the angle; the smallest opening, 2·asin(m/E) = 133.8°, is for a decay perpendicular to the X17 direction. A decay along the motion stays at 180°. Because the decay is isotropic (flat in cos θ*) and the curve is flat near cos θ* = 0, most decays land just above the minimum.

The recoil of the whole ⁸Be* is a second, much smaller boost. The toy MC in appendix_calc.py (2×10⁵ isotropic X17 decays, boosted along the beam by β = 0.0059) gives the numbers above. MEG II also neglects it. Tables: out/appendix/x17_decay.csv, boost.csv, boost_dtheta.csv.

A real particle must move with E_p; a mass shift moves it the other way. The IPC shape (and cosmics) do not move. Scanning E_p is the cleanest test there is.

ATOMKI 2016 saw no excess at 17.64 MeV. Hanoi (1.225 MeV) found m = 16.66 ± 0.47 ± 0.35 MeV, consistent with 2016 at a different E_p.

lnl/out/acceptance_hist.csv (generated columns), lnl/out/kinematics.csv

31

Details

θ_min = 2·asin(m_X/E_X): with the mass fixed, a larger E_X means a larger velocity and a smaller minimum angle. E_X is E* (the ⁸Be ground-state recoil takes negligible energy), and E* follows E_p with slope 7/8. Over the 0.44–1.23 MeV programme, E* goes 17.64 → 18.33 MeV and the edge from 142° to 131° (m = 16.7). Main slide 5 plots θ_min against E_p for three masses.

The width of the distribution is the same kinematics: the faster the X17, the wider the range from θ_min to 180°. At 17.64 MeV the X17 moves slowest (β = 0.32) and the pairs crowd into 140–150°.

On resonance for rate; off resonance to test the X17

Thin-target γ₀ rate against E_p, split into the 18.15 MeV resonance and direct capture. Hover the points.

No: off resonance is not more X17. The total γ₀ is lowest there, and the E1 IPC it leaves is worse at 140°. Off-resonance points are tests, not yield.

lnl/out/appendix/offres.csv; days: lnl/out/geant/reach_geant.csv (MM 15° + TOF, m = 16.7)

32

Details

The question from main slide 4: if half the γ₀ at 1.1 MeV is direct E1 capture, should we sit where E1 dominates to get more X17? It depends on what the X17 couples to, which is exactly what is unknown:

  1. X17 from the 1⁺ resonance only (the 2016 picture: an M1-like emission from the 18.15 MeV state). Then the X17 rate is the orange curve × R, which falls to ~zero off resonance. Off-resonance runs should show nothing.
  2. X17 from any transition at the same R (ATOMKI 2022 claim an excess in direct capture too; this is what the main deck's reach assumes). Then the X17 follows the black curve, which is highest on the resonance and 19 % / -7 % lower at 0.80 / 1.225 MeV.

In both cases the rate is best at ~1.03–1.10 MeV. Off resonance, the background is also worse: the leftover E1 IPC makes ~2.9× more pairs per photon at 140° than M1 (C2). Hence the table: 0.80 and 1.225 MeV take ×3.5 and ×3.8 longer than 1.10 as built.

The value of the off-resonance points is that they separate hypotheses 1 and 2, and that the edge moves with E_p (C5). A sensible plan: calibrate at 441 keV (pure M1, known shape), take most data at 1.03–1.10 MeV, then 0.80 and 1.225 MeV.

Curve: out/appendix/offres.csv (lnl_rates.thin_yield at each E_p, Li₂O 300 µg/cm²). The x axis is the energy entering the film; the peak sits ~30 keV above 1030 keV because the film is 60 keV thick. The wiggle of the direct-capture curve under the resonance is an artefact of subtracting constant-width Breit–Wigners from the Zahnow data (main slide 4); only the sum is measured. The 0.80 MeV row of the table is ATOMKI's LiF 300 target, so its rate is lower than this Li₂O curve.
